ICJ is due to rule on the Rohingya genocide case. Here's what you need to know
item.description:
ICJ is due to rule on the Rohingya genocide case. Here's what you need to know

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Thu, 11/05/2026 - 11:06
UN's top court sets 19 November as date for landmark judgment in case brought by Gambia against Myanmar
Off

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, in a judgment that could see the court hold a state responsible for genocide for the first time.

Officials announced on Tuesday that the court's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, would read the judgment at a public sitting at the Peace Palace in The Hague at 10am local time on 19 November. 

The ruling will be final and binding, with no right of appeal.

Several governments have already described the violence as genocide, including the US and Canada.

Legal experts say they expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people.

The case, brought by the Gambia in 2019, concerns the Myanmar military's 2017 violence in Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighbouring Bangladesh and involved widely documented massacres and rapes. 

About 1.2 million Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority, now live in camps around Cox's Bazar, the world's largest refugee settlement.

Myanmar has denied committing genocide, saying its forces were responding to insurgents from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa), whose attacks on police posts in August 2017 killed 12 security personnel.

Antonia Mulvey, an international human rights lawyer who investigated sexual violence against the Rohingya for the UN in 2017, told Middle East Eye's Expert Witness Podcast that horrific sexual violence was central to the Gambia's argument that genocide took place.

"One individual said to me, 'I was lucky, I was only raped by three men,'" said Mulvey, whose organisation, Legal Action Worldwide, now represents Rohingya witnesses in the case.

"They would rape women and girls in public, in front of their family members, in front of their children, in communal areas. I heard of mass gang rapes, sometimes up to 40 women and girls at the time."

What is the case about?

The Gambia accuses Myanmar of breaching the 1948 Genocide Convention during its campaign against the Rohingya from 25 August 2017. 

The operations were carried out under Min Aung Hlaing, then the military's commander-in-chief. 

Myanmar at the time had a civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, but the military-drafted constitution left the armed forces outside its control.

In February 2021, Min Aung Hlaing overthrew Suu Kyi's government in a coup, and in April this year he stepped down as army chief.

He was later elected president by a parliament dominated by military-backed lawmakers, following elections organised by the junta.

Rohingya fled mass killings, rape and the burning of villages during what the military described as "clearance operations".

The case is a dispute between states, so the court will decide whether Myanmar as a state is responsible, not whether any individual is guilty. 

A finding against Myanmar would arguably add to international pressure on Min Aung Hlaing, whose move to the presidency is widely perceived as a bid for international legitimacy.

How did it start?

In 2018, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar concluded that there was sufficient information to infer genocidal intent and recommended that senior military officials be investigated and prosecuted for genocide.

On 11 November 2019, the Gambia filed its case at the ICJ with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). 

The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide
Read More »

It was the first time a state not directly affected had brought a genocide case before the court. 

The west African country relied on the principle that every state party to the 1948 Genocide Convention has a common interest in seeing it upheld.

In December 2019, Aung San Suu Kyi, then Myanmar's civilian leader, appeared at the court to deny the allegations. 

In January 2020, after finding “a real and imminent risk of irreparable prejudice to the rights” of the Rohingya under the Genocide Convention, the court ordered Myanmar to prevent genocidal acts and preserve evidence.

The court rejected Myanmar's objections to its jurisdiction in July 2022, and heard the merits of the case from 12-29 January 2026, including closed-door testimony from Rohingya witnesses.

Eleven states have intervened: Belgium, Canada, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, France, Germany, the Republic of Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom.

Mike Becker, an assistant professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin and a former associate legal officer at the ICJ, told MEE the judgment would be the first merits judgment in a case with large-scale intervention by third states.

"Cases like the Gambia v Myanmar have arguably sought to transform the role and function of the ICJ in contemporary affairs. The outcome here may determine whether that trend will continue," Becker said.

What are the arguments?

The Gambia argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the Myanmar military's conduct. 

It relied on four acts listed in the convention: killing; causing serious bodily or mental harm; inflicting conditions of life calculated to destroy the group; and measures intended to prevent births.

Mulvey said the Gambia pointed to around 10,000 killings, which she described as a conservative estimate, and to decades of restrictions on Rohingya marriage, births, movement and access to healthcare.

Myanmar denies genocide. It argues the operations were a counterterrorism response to Arsa, that there is no direct evidence of intent, and that the UN fact-finding mission's reports should not be given evidentiary weight.

Myanmar has submitted 12 reports on its compliance with the 2020 order. The Gambia has said these give "no reason to conclude" that Myanmar complied.

Why is sexual violence central?

Mulvey said she documented a consistent pattern across the townships of Maungdaw, Buthidaung and Rathedaung, in which soldiers surrounded villages, opened fire, set homes alight and then selected women and girls for rape.

She said survivors described gang rapes carried out in public and in front of their families, women held in military camps for weeks, mutilation, and soldiers telling them: "We will kill you by raping you."

One woman told Mulvey she had been eight months pregnant when she was hanged from a tree and raped by nine men, most of them soldiers. Her unborn child died. Her account was included in the fact-finding mission's report and later read out at the ICJ.

The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda ruled in 1998 that rape can constitute genocide. The ICJ has accepted the principle, but has never found a state responsible on that basis.

Mulvey said such a finding would be "a landmark decision".

"It was the scale and the brutality of the sexual violence that we didn't see in previous cases before the International Court of Justice, such as before Bosnia and Croatia," she said.

Why does it matter under international law?

The judgment will be only the third time the ICJ has ruled on the merits of a genocide case, and the first in more than a decade.

In 2007, the court found that genocide was committed at Srebrenica but held Serbia responsible only for failing to prevent and punish it.

'It was the scale and the brutality of the sexual violence that we didn't see in previous cases before the International Court of Justice'

– Antonia Mulvey, human rights lawyer

In 2015, it found that genocide had not been proven in Croatia's case against Serbia.

Furthermore, how the court applies the “only reasonable inference” test is expected to be a central legal question addressed by the judgment. 

The test governs how genocidal intent, meaning the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part, can be proven when there is no direct evidence of it, such as an explicit order or policy document. In this case, it would require proving whether any explanation other than genocide could reasonably account for what happened in Rakhine.

The Gambia argues that the scale, pattern and brutality of the 2017 operations meet that test. 

It points to the mass killings, the systematic rape of women and girls, and decades of discriminatory policies against the Rohingya.

“Here we don’t have a physical document that shows that, but it was the whole pattern that we saw,” Mulvey said.

Myanmar argues that other reasonable inferences can be drawn, chiefly that its forces were conducting counterterrorism operations against Arsa.

At the January hearings, its counsel also argued that the military’s aim was to drive the Rohingya out of the country, not to destroy them.

Chris Sidoti, a former member of the UN fact-finding mission on Myanmar, told MEE that the ruling would also show how the court approaches establishing facts and the weight given to reports from UN human rights mechanisms.

"The International Court of Justice is not a fact-finding tribunal. It doesn't have an investigative arm, and mostly it makes decisions that are purely legal questions," said Sidoti, who now sits on the UN Commission of Inquiry on Palestine and Israel. "Here it's got a fact-finding task ahead of it."

Will the ICJ lower the genocide threshold?

In October, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz accused Navi Pillay, the Nobel Peace laureate and the ad hoc judge appointed by the Gambia, of "tipping the scales", saying she intended to lower the threshold for proving genocide so it could be used against America and its allies.

Mulvey rejected the claim as "misleading".

"The Gambia is very clear in its submissions; they are not asking the court to lower the threshold [for genocide]. Rather, they are saying the threshold has been met," she said.

What do the victims want?

Rohingya survivors want the court to find Myanmar responsible for genocide and to order the return of their land and property, compensation and prosecutions. 

Above all, they want citizenship, which they are denied under Myanmar's 1982 citizenship law, said Mulvey. 

If the court finds Myanmar responsible, it will also find that Myanmar must make reparation to the Rohingya, though it may defer the question of remedies to a later phase, Becker said.

The remedy the court orders "could be groundbreaking, especially if the ICJ requires Myanmar to undertake domestic reforms to guarantee basic rights of citizenship and non-discrimination to the Rohingya", he said.

"Decades on, they don't forget what has happened to them or to their families," Mulvey said. "At the very minimum, they want recognition."

What happens next?

Myanmar is bound to comply with the judgment. If it does not, the Gambia can refer the matter to the UN Security Council, which has never used its power to enforce an ICJ ruling.

Becker said enforcement may prove impossible while the military remains in power, but "compliance with the ICJ judgment may become the price of readmission to the international community". 

A finding against Myanmar could also increase pressure on other states to disengage from the ICJ, he said.

Myanmar has been embroiled in civil war since the 2021 coup, and the Arakan Army, an ethnic armed group, now controls most of Rakhine State.

Separately, the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court applied in November 2024 for an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing, then the military's commander-in-chief, over the deportation and persecution of the Rohingya. Judges have not publicly ruled on the request.

“We want to see that arrest warrant issued, and also that arrest warrants are requested for other senior members of the Myanmar military,” Mulvey said.

In February 2025, a court in Argentina ordered arrest warrants for 25 Myanmar officials, including Min Aung Hlaing and Aung San Suu Kyi, in a case brought under the legal principle that atrocity crimes can be prosecuted anywhere. 

Because the court relies on precedents as part of its sources, the case will have implications on the other genocide-related cases pending before the ICJ: Ukraine v Russia, South Africa v Israel, Nicaragua v Germany and the Democratic Republic of the Congo v Rwanda.

item.title: Bangladesh Bank relaxes rules to allow Tk 30b loan to City Group
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has suspended a provision of the Bank Company Act to facilitate a Tk 30 billion working capital loan to five defaulting companies of City Group, one of the country's leading industrial conglomerates.

According to a Bangladesh Bank notification, the five loan-defaulting companies of City Group are City Seed Crushing Industries Ltd, City Sugar Industries Ltd, City Edible Oil Ltd, City Dal Mills Ltd and Shampa Flour Mills Ltd.

The relevant provision of the Bank Company Act will not apply to the syndicated financing, led by City Bank, to provide working capital facilities worth Tk 30 billion to these companies.

Bangladesh Bank issued a notification today granting the exemption.

Section 27KaKa(3) of the Bank Company Act has been suspended for City Group until December next year. Under this provision, a loan-defaulting company is not eligible to obtain fresh loans.

Bangladesh Bank Deputy Governor Kabir Ahmed issued the notification suspending the provision until December next year. As a result, City Group, which markets products under the Teer brand, will face no further regulatory hurdles in obtaining fresh loans.

At a meeting held at Bangladesh Bank on 25 October, the central bank advised the lending banks not to classify City Group's loans as defaulted at this stage. It also suggested that the conglomerate be given facilities for long-term loan restructuring and rescheduling, if necessary, to help it overcome its difficulties and resume normal operations.

In addition, an initiative was taken to form a consortium of the lending banks to provide the conglomerate with the working capital needed to continue its business.

The group owes more than Tk 260 billion to 43 banks, and these loans have already become classified as defaulted. Bangladesh Bank Governor Mostakur Rahman, top executives of several lending banks and City Group Managing Director Md Hasan attended the tripartite meeting at the central bank.

The notification issued today also sets out several conditions.

It states that neither the government nor Bangladesh Bank will incur any liability arising from the proposed loan facility. In the future, City Bank or any other bank or financial institution participating in the consortium will not be entitled to seek any form of financial assistance from the government or Bangladesh Bank.

To ensure adequate collateral against the proposed loan facility, City Group will provide registered mortgages on properties that are not already encumbered by any of its other loans or liabilities.

The proceeds from selling goods purchased with the syndicated loan must be deposited into a designated bank account. Payments to the participating banks against the syndicated loan facility must then be made regularly from that account on a proportionate basis, with priority given to settling their dues.

The notification further states that the raw materials imported using the syndicated loan will be purchased by the lending banks of the borrowing companies, acting through a security agent, and processed under their custody.

LDC graduation is deferred by three years. Does it make things better?
item.description:
Last December, I argued in this column that Bangladesh should graduate from least developed country status on schedule in 2026. I argued against deferral for three reasons.
First , it sends a wrong signal to the investors, that even though we passed all the markers for graduation we are not ready to accept it, which means our fundamentals remained weak and the economy was weaker than we had been projecting.
Second , the delay would fix nothing. We would be buying time but time does not fix our woes.
Third , I asked that the debate shifts from when or whether to graduate to preparing for graduation so that we benefit from it.
For me, LDC graduation is a stress test. But the deferral has happened and we now have three years. Does it make things better or worse?
The resolution grants the extension on an exceptional basis, and the graduation framework does not treat a domestic political transition as grounds for one. This was a concession and it is not a precedent.
Attached to it is an obligation to implement a national smooth transition strategy and report progress to the Committee for Development Policy every year. The Committee has also revised its supplementary indicators for the 2027 review to a set of 44, calling the change a shift from once-off measurement to continuous assessment.
We will be judged every year, in public, on a trajectory rather than a snapshot, and no stated ground is left on which to ask for more time.
What is the case for the deferral?
Merchandise exports were $48 billion in FY2025-26, of which readymade garments accounted for $38.70bn, about four-fifths of our export.
The European Union took $19.06bn of those garment exports. Nearly three-quarters of everything we sell abroad moves under duty-free terms we hold only because we are a least developed country, and that share has to find new terms by 2029.
Two things change when that access ends; the tariff is the smaller of them. The first is the rule of origin.
Everything But Arms lets imported fabric made up into garments here qualify as ours, while standard preferences require both the fabric and the garment to be made in Bangladesh.
We import about 60% of our woven fabric, so a large part of the woven trade would fail that test and bear the full tariff whichever scheme we sit under.
The second change is the duty itself, as European Union tariffs on apparel run at about 11.8% at the most-favoured-nation rate and 9.6% under standard preferences, against zero today.
The published estimates of what this costs differ by a factor of three. UNCTAD's Trade Preferences Outlook 2025 puts the annual loss above $17.5bn, a fall of 32%, with 77% of it in the European Union alone.
SANEM puts it near 11% of exports and the UN readiness assessment at between 5.5% and 15%, where UNCTAD's own earlier modelling also sat.
The spread is not a dispute about arithmetic. It turns on whether our garments pay the full tariff or fall back on standard preferences.
Against last year's $48bn, the bill is somewhere between $2.6bn and more than $17bn a year, and we are preparing without knowing which.
Our external position is already resting on remittances rather than on exports. The trade deficit reached $27.28bn in FY2025-26 and the current account closed about $1.6bn in deficit. Record remittances of $35.6bn held reserves at $36.21bn in mid-October. An export loss at the modest end of those estimates lands on that arithmetic, as no second earner can absorb it.
The timing is worse than the amount. External debt stood at $78.22bn in March and 62% of it is concessional. Debt service rises from $4.11bn in FY25 to a projected $7.6bn by FY29, the year the preferences end, and graduation closes the windows that made the debt cheap.
The debt is already about 140% of annual exports, and that ratio worsens from both directions if exports fall while servicing rises at market rates.
Last December, the IMF put our growth near 3.5% with inflation easing. In October, it cut the projection for this year to 3.2%, the weakest since 1988-89, and raised inflation to 10.9%.
The World Bank expects the weakness to persist through FY28, two of the three years we have been given, and private sector credit growth fell to 4.5% in June, a 33-year low.
A diversified export base is built out of investment in laboratories, certification, cold chain, and reliable power, and none of that is financed out of 3.2% growth.
First , the choice is not ours. Graduation follows from meeting the thresholds at two consecutive reviews, and at the 2024 review our income per head stood at $2,684 against a threshold of $1,306, the Human Assets Index at 77.5 against 66, and the vulnerability index at 21.9 where 32 or below qualifies. A government can ask for time, which we have now done, and after that the question is closed.
Second , the preferences are worth less every year even if we keep them, as a margin of preference is only the gap between our duty and our competitors'. Vietnam already sells into the European Union under a trade agreement and India is negotiating one, so that gap narrows on its own.
Third, the preferences shape what we make. They apply to the goods we already produce, so they reward more of the same, and a quarter-century of duty-free access to Europe has left one sector supplying four-fifths of exports. A country off the list negotiates agreements instead of receiving concessions, and an agreement can be written for a product we do not yet sell. The loss above is the price of the transition rather than a permanent cut in what we can earn.
First , the Ministry of Commerce should obtain a written position from the European Commission, before the 2027 review, on whether our apparel qualifies for GSP+ or standard preferences. On Mohiuddin Rubel's reading of the safeguard threshold, it qualifies for neither, and every other decision depends on the answer.
Second , the government should ratify the outstanding conventions required for GSP+ and file the first implementation reports by December 2027, as the scheme rests on a record of enforcement.
Third , the Ministry of Textiles should publish an annual target for domestically produced woven fabric, beginning this fiscal year, as the origin rule applies to the fabric rather than to the duty.
Fourth , it should bring the agreements with Japan and South Korea into force by December 2027 and conclude one more by the end of 2028.
Fifth , the national accreditation board should secure European recognition of its certificates by 2028, as a buyer who will not accept our test report needs no tariff to refuse our goods.
Sixth , the Directorate General of Drug Administration should settle licensing before November 2029 for the fifth to a quarter of locally made medicines patented abroad, as a 4% royalty adds 2% to 3% to the price of a generic.
Seventh , the Ministry of Finance should release the annual progress report at home when it submits it to the Committee, stating the target, the deadline and the responsible ministry for each item above.
Every one of the seven can be completed before November 2029, provided each has a named ministry and a date set against it in writing. Otherwise the three years will pass as the past year has.
Md Rubaiyath Sarwar is Managing Director of Innovision Consulting, a Trustee of Panam Institute.

ECNEC approves 13 projects worth Tk58088.92cr; govt to drill 2 new gas wells
item.description:
The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) on Wednesday approved a total of 13 development projects with an estimated cost of Tk58,088.92 crore, including a fresh project to drill two new gas wells at Tk592 crore for availing 30 mmcfd.
Prime Minister and ECNEC Chairman Tarique Rahman presided over the sixth ECNEC meeting of the current fiscal year (FY27) at the Cabinet Room of Bangladesh Secretariat on Wednesday.
Of the approved 13 projects, 11 are new while two are revised projects.
Of the total estimated cost of Tk58,088.92 crore, the government will provide Tk50,041.20 crore, Tk73.07 crore will come from concerned organization’s own funds, while the rest of Tk7,974.65 crore from project assistance.
State Minister for Planning Md Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki briefed reporters after the meeting at the NEC Conference Room in the city’s Sher-e-Bangla Nagar area.
According to the Planning Commission, the government will drill two appraisal-cum-development wells at the Titas Gas Field at an estimated cost of Tk592 crore to increase domestic gas production by around 30 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd).
The project titled "Drilling of Two Appraisal-cum-Development Wells (Titas-32 and Titas-33) at Titas Gas Field" will be implemented by the Bangladesh Gas Fields Company Limited (BGFCL), a Petrobangla subsidiary, under the Energy and Mineral Resources Division of the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources till September 2029.
Of the total estimated cost, Tk414.40 crore will come from government financing and Tk177.60 crore from the company's own funds.
The government has set a target to drill 150 wells by 2031 to raise gas output, followed by another 150 wells during the 2031-'35 period to further strengthen the country's local gas production.
According to the proposal, the wells could produce around 100.74 billion cubic feet (BCF) of gas and 60,444 barrels of condensate over 10 years. The estimated value of the output at the company's existing wellhead prices stands at Tk339.07 crore, including Tk285.26 crore for gas and Tk53.81 crore for condensate.
At consumer-level gas prices, the estimated value of the gas output over the same period would be Tk6,523.97 crore.
BGFCL currently supplies around 480-485 million cubic feet of gas daily to the national grid from five of its six operational gas fields. The Titas Gas Field, the company's largest, produces around 330 million cubic feet daily from 23 of its 28 drilled wells.
The project follows a review of three-dimensional seismic survey data collected at the Titas and Bakhrabad gas fields during 2010-2012. BGFCL engaged BGP Inc. of China National Petroleum Corporation to review the data. The consultant recommended drilling 16 infill wells and seven deep wells.
The government has prioritised Titas-32 and Titas-33 under its plan to drill 150 onshore gas wells to increase domestic production.
The project will cover drilling the two wells through a foreign contractor, engaging local and foreign consultants, installing gas-gathering pipelines and carrying out related works.
The Infrastructure Investment Facilitation Company (IIFC) conducted the feasibility study in 2026. The Planning Commission said the project would support domestic gas production, industrial development and foreign exchange savings by reducing LNG imports.
The proposal was revised following a Project Evaluation Committee meeting held on June 18, 2026, which recommended rationalising project costs. The estimated cost was reduced by Tk40 crore from the initial proposal of Tk632 crore to Tk592 crore.
In the day’s meeting, the Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Ministry secured approval for five projects, while the Home Ministry received approval for two projects. The Ministries of Defence, Housing and Public Works, Science and Technology, Education, Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, and Disaster Management and Relief received approval for one project each.
Planning Ministry officials said the 13 projects include initiatives covering safe water supply and sanitation in the Barind region with Taka 1,203.73 crore, re-excavation of canals in Barishal City Corporation, and local economic development in selected municipalities with Tk730.66 crore.
The three other projects under the Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Ministry include Innovation for Climate-Smart Urban Development Project with Tk87.40 crore; Social Infrastructure Development Project (SIDP) with Tk2,565.59 crore and the Priority Basis Important Rural Infrastructure Development Project-03 (Third Revision) with an additional cost of Tk3,951.37 crore.
The two projects approved under the Home Ministry involve the procurement of specialised vehicles and operational vehicles to enhance the capacity of Bangladesh Police.
The Defence Ministry will implement a project to construct Type-B officers’ residential accommodation in the Moinul Road residential area of Dhaka Cantonment with Tk177.19 crore.
The Housing and Public Works Ministry will construct multi-storey residential buildings for government employees at Gabtala Colony in Jigatala with Taka 200.11 crore.
The Science and Technology Ministry will establish Institutes of Nuclear Medicine and Allied Sciences (INMAS) on the campuses of five medical college hospitals across the country with Tk535.54 crore.
The Education Ministry received approval for the Fifth Primary Education Development Programme (PEDP-5) with Tk41,090.48 crore.
The Disaster Management and Relief Ministry will implement the third revised project for constructing bridges and culverts up to 15 metres in length on rural roads with an additional cost of Tk523.34 crore.
Meanwhile, the meeting was informed about five projects costing less than Tk50 crore each that the planning minister had already approved.
The projects include the modernisation of cardiac treatment services at Zia Heart Foundation Hospital and Research Institute in Dinajpur; ensuring safe internet use for children, adolescents and secondary-level students; improvement of traffic infrastructure and road safety in Dhaka North City Corporation (first revision); expansion and modernisation of the Dhaka Central Drug Addiction Treatment Centre (first revision); and procurement of modern vehicles and equipment to improve waste management in Gazipur City Corporation.
Ministers, advisers to the prime minister, and state ministers concerned attended the meeting, while Planning Commission members and secretaries concerned were present.

item.title: Garment unrest eases after eight days as workers return to factories
item.description:
The garment sector showed signs of returning to normal on Thursday after eight days of unrest over minimum wages, with workers resuming production across major industrial belts in Savar, Gazipur and Narayanganj, although sporadic protests in Ashulia forced 70 factories to suspend operations.
The improvement came after days of demonstrations, clashes with police and widespread factory closures that disrupted production in the country’s largest export-earning industry.
While most factories resumed operations, uncertainty over the proposed minimum wage continued to fuel isolated demonstrations, particularly in Ashulia, where workers blocked roads and clashed with police.
Authorities reinforced security across industrial areas, deploying 33 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) to prevent further disruptions and facilitate the resumption of factory operations.
The government has already formed a wage board to review workers’ pay, with a revised wage structure expected to take effect in December.
However, the amount of the proposed increase has yet to be announced.
Workers have been demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, arguing that rising living costs have made their existing salaries inadequate.
Factories in Savar and the Dhaka Export Processing Zone (DEPZ) resumed production Thursday morning after several days of disruption.
Workers entered their workplaces peacefully, while additional police and BGB personnel remained stationed outside important industrial establishments in Ashulia and Hemayetpur.
Normal operations also resumed across much of Gazipur, including Shafipur, Chandra and Palli Bidyut in Kaliakair, as well as Bhogra Bypass, Konabari, Kashimpur and Salna.
Workers joined their respective shifts without major disruption, bringing relief to factory management after several days of uncertainty.
The situation in Narayanganj also remained largely calm, with workers returning to their workplaces.
Despite the broader improvement, Ashulia witnessed fresh demonstrations as workers continued demanding clarity over the proposed wage increase.
Workers at several factories initially joined their shifts around 8am and registered attendance before leaving their workplaces and gathering outside nearby factories.
Some demonstrators urged workers from neighbouring establishments to join the protests, prompting factory authorities to suspend operations.
Industrial Police-1 Superintendent Mominul Islam Bhuiyan said 70 of the 1,863 factories under his jurisdiction had declared holidays, while the remaining factories continued operating.
He described the overall situation as stable despite isolated disturbances.
Protesters blocked the Abdullahpur-Baipail road, disrupting traffic before police intervened to clear the highway.
Clashes subsequently erupted in Jamgora, where some protesters allegedly threw bricks and stones at police and vandalised police vehicles.
Police used tear gas and sound grenades to disperse the demonstrators.
Mominul said the unrest began after some workers were dismissed and police detained several individuals during the demonstrations.
He also alleged that outsiders were attempting to provoke workers and disrupt factory operations, including through social media.
Authorities deployed 33 BGB platoons across major industrial areas as part of efforts to maintain order and prevent further disruption.
According to BGB headquarters, three platoons were deployed in Mirpur, 11 in Savar and Ashulia, 12 in Gazipur and seven in Narayanganj.
Armoured personnel carriers, riot control vehicles and drones were being used to strengthen security and monitor developments.
BGB personnel were also equipped with body-worn cameras, while a monitoring cell at headquarters was overseeing the situation around the clock.
Meanwhile, the Detective Branch arrested eight more people in connection with Tuesday’s attack on police during garment workers’ demonstrations in Mirpur-11.
DMP Deputy Commissioner Md Akhtar Hossain said investigators identified the suspects through CCTV footage and technological assistance.
Although production has resumed in most industrial areas, the dispute over wages remains unresolved.
The government has formed a minimum wage board and announced plans to introduce a revised wage structure from December, but workers have yet to receive confirmation of the proposed minimum amount.
Industrial Police officials said factory owners were committed to implementing the revised structure once finalised.
The latest developments follow protests that began in Mirpur on October 29 and subsequently spread to Ashulia, Gazipur, Savar and Narayanganj.
The demonstrations triggered repeated clashes, road blockades and temporary factory closures, with at least 529 factories suspending production at one stage.
“In Sha Allah, the board (newly formed wage board) will set a new minimum wage within the next one to two months so that our dear workers can live a little better.”

item.title: World Bank: Bangladesh’s external debt rises to $113.4bn
item.description:
Bangladesh’s total external debt climbed 8.6 percent to reach $113.4 billion in 2025, according to the World Bank’s International Debt Report 2026, even as the country maintained manageable debt-to-GNI and debt-service ratios amid a broader global financing squeeze.
The new report reveals that Bangladesh’s long-term public and publicly guaranteed (PPG) external debt stands at $89.5 billion. Multilateral creditors hold the majority share of these public obligations at $51.1 billion—primarily driven by the World Bank’s International Development Association ($22.6 billion) and the Asian Development Bank ($17.5 billion).
Bilateral debt accounts for $32.6 billion, anchored by major partners like Japan ($12.7 billion) and the Russian Federation ($9.0 billion).
Private nonguaranteed debt of $9.9 billion and $14.1 billion in short-term liabilities make up the remainder of the nation's external profile.
Despite the rising debt stock, Bangladesh’s macro-fiscal indicators reflect resilience compared to regional peers.
The country's external debt-to-GNI ratio stood at a moderate 24 percent, while the debt service-to-exports ratio eased by 3.1% to 16%.
Official commitments extended to Bangladesh also retained favorable terms, featuring an average maturity of 25 years, a 6-year grace period, and an average interest rate of 3%.
Zooming out to the regional picture, total external debt across South Asia reached $955 billion in 2025.
While regional debt-to-GNI ratios remain contained at an average of 21 percent, South Asian economies face an increasingly unforgiving global capital environment.
On a global scale, total external debt across all low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) surged 5.5% to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, marking the sharpest increase in four years as private lenders and bond markets forcefully reopened.
However, this renewed market access has come at an exorbitant price, particularly for the poorest economies. Private creditors charged IDA-eligible countries an average interest rate of 8.2% on new commitments in 2025—the highest level seen since the late 1980s.
Total debt service payments for LMICs rose for the fifth consecutive year to $1.4 trillion, consuming over 40% of government revenues in vulnerable nations and crowding out vital spending on health, education, and infrastructure.
Commenting on the global outlook, World Bank Chief Statistician Haishan Fu warned that access to finance is not enough.
“We must know the debt, understand its terms, and ensure that the financing developing economies receive strengthens rather than constrains their ability to grow, withstand shocks, and improve the lives of their people."
Adding to this, World Bank analysts noted a troubling paradox where developing nations are borrowing more and paying steeper prices, ultimately leaving fewer resources available for long-term sustainable development.

item.title: July atrocities: ICT accepts charges against Amu, 6 others
item.description:
The International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) on Thursday took cognisance of charges against seven individuals linked to the Awami League, including former minister Amir Hossain Amu, in a case filed over crimes against humanity committed during the July 2024 uprising.
The three-member bench of the ICT-2, led by Justice Nozrul Islam Chowdhury, also ordered that six of the accused, who were in jail, be produced before it on November 22 in connection with the case.
It issued a warrant for the arrest of Awami League Organising Secretary Mirza Azam, who had been absconding.
The other accused in the cases were former Shipping Minister Shajahan Khan, former Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister Lt Col (retd) Faruk Khan, former Agricultural Minister Abdur Razzaque, former minister Dr Dipu Moni and former Energy Adviser to the ousted Prime Minister Tawfiq-e-Elahi Chowdhury.
Briefing reporters, Prosecutor Gazi Tamim said former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina had taken state-level and political decisions to suppress the July mass uprising.
Plans had been devised to use lethal weapons against protesters, impose a curfew, shut down the internet and control the media, he said.
Records of conversations, documents, supporting evidence and witness statements had been submitted to the tribunal in support of these allegations, Tamim added.
He said various pieces of evidence, including a United Nations report, had been submitted to support allegations that state forces and intelligence agencies had been used to carry out killings to suppress the movement.
The prosecutor also claimed that the UN report had contained an alleged instruction by Sheikh Hasina to "kill them and hide the bodies."
Regarding the individual roles of the accused, he said the prosecution had presented information that Tk 5 crore in cash had been found in sacks at the residence of Amu after August 5, 2024.
Faruk Khan attended a security committee meeting on August 4, where a decision had allegedly been taken to shoot and kill protesters at the entry points to Dhaka on August 5, according to the prosecution.
Dipu Moni, meanwhile, had participated in a meeting on imposing the curfew and had been involved in planning to suppress the movement, Tamim alleged.
He also claimed that Shajahan Khan, through conversations with Sheikh Hasina, had issued instructions to deploy police, Awami League leaders and activists, and workers against the protesters.
The case also includes allegations of arson at various establishments during the movement.
The prosecutor said recordings of conversations involving Sheikh Hasina, Obaidul Quader and Hasan Mahmud had been submitted to the tribunal in this regard.
Forensic reports verifying the authenticity of the recordings, along with video reports verified by experts from the BBC, Al Jazeera and the United Nations, had also been submitted, he added.
Tamim said the seven accused had been charged with incitement, assistance, conspiracy and contribution to the commission of crimes. They also face allegations of superior command responsibility.
The prosecution alleged that the accused, from their respective positions, played roles in making and implementing political decisions to suppress the movement.
The prosecutor further said the investigation into the abduction and torture of six coordinators of the July uprising while in the custody of the Detective Branch (DB) was nearing completion.
Earlier, on November 2, the prosecution submitted formal charges against the seven leaders.

item.title: Humaiun Kobir: Bangladesh wants Hasina extradited from India
item.description:
Referring to the existing extradition treaty with India, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Thursday said they want former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who now faces the death penalty, to be handed over to Bangladesh.
“We want Hasina to be handed over. She will be handed over. She is a terrorist. She is a fled criminal. There is an active extradition treaty between Bangladesh and India,” he told reporters, noting that there is no need to issue her a passport.
Kobir made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport after seeing off Liu Haixing, Minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee.
Hasina, ousted in a mass uprising in 2024, has told The Associated Press that she remains committed to returning to Bangladesh from exile in India next month, despite being sentenced to death over her government's deadly crackdown on protesters.
“If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” she told AP in response to questions by email. “So, I will return to Bangladesh. That decision has not changed.”
Hasina fled to India after student-led protests forced her from power and has remained there ever since.
In 2025, a Bangladeshi special tribunal sentenced her to death for crimes against humanity, ruling that she was responsible for ordering the crackdown, which left hundreds of people dead and thousands of others injured.
Bangladesh has repeatedly sought Hasina’s extradition, but India has declined to hand her over. She first announced in August her intention to return in December.
On October 3, Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi stressed that former Prime Minister Hasina was not brought to India by the Indian Air Force or the Indian Army. He said the legal process concerning Bangladesh’s request for her extradition was ongoing and that no timeframe could be given as the courts were involved.
“To give you a straight answer, again and again, the government of India, through the Spokesperson at the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), has replied to this that there is a process, and the process involves legality, and it is well structured. So, as far as that is concerned, the process is on,” Trivedi said.
He said the courts were involved in the matter and, therefore, “nobody can give you a timeframe.”
Trivedi said Hasina was still the Prime Minister of Bangladesh when she arrived in India, and New Delhi had to respond to the situation as a neighboring country.
“At that point in time, Hasina was still the prime minister of Bangladesh. We had hardly any choice on that. It was our duty as a neighbor to accept the reality of life, because situations are such where at times you are not prepared for it,” the Indian envoy said.
Trivedi also referred to the circumstances under which Hasina came to India after leaving Bangladesh in August 2024, saying the Indian authorities were not prepared for the situation.
“Going back to history, Hasina Ji was not brought to India by the Indian Air Force or Indian Army,” he said, referring to the circumstances surrounding her departure from Bangladesh.
He said the situation unfolded because of “tragic circumstances” in Bangladesh at the time, adding that such circumstances should never be repeated anywhere in the world, where innocent people get killed, regardless of which part of the world it is.
He questioned what India's alternative could have been under those circumstances. “What was our choice? If you would have said that no, we are not going to accept, we don’t give landing permission. Things would have been I don’t know what,” Trivedi said.
Bangladesh has repeatedly requested India to extradite Hasina, who has been staying in India since her departure from Bangladesh in August 2024.
The issue was also raised by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman during his meeting with Trivedi in Dhaka in August.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs subsequently said that Bangladesh’s request was being examined in line with established procedures.

item.title: PM lays foundation stone for Tk4,068cr Mongla Port project
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday laid the foundation stone for a Tk4,068 crore project to construct two container jetties and develop supporting infrastructure to expand and modernise Mongla Port.
He laid the foundation stone at a ceremony in Mongla, Bagerhat, at 11:15am, said Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Jahidul Islam Rony.
The project aims to expand the port's capacity and modernise its facilities through the construction of two container jetties and the development of associated infrastructure.
Earlier in the morning, the Prime Minister arrived in Mongla by helicopter around 9:50am to attend a series of programmes as part of his daylong visit to Bagerhat and Khulna.
After the arrival, Tarique attended the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Invest Bangladesh and China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) on economic and infrastructure cooperation in Mongla.
On behalf of Invest Bangladesh, its Member (Industrial Zone) Saleh Ahmed signed the agreement, while China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation Chairman Li Chongyang signed it on behalf of the Chinese side.
Under the MoU, the two sides will explore investment opportunities in key sectors, including energy, industrial infrastructure, green infrastructure, transport, logistics and human resource development.

India makes visa mandatory for 6 minority groups from Bangladesh, Afghanistan, Pakistan
item.description:
India has made it mandatory for members of six non-Muslim communities from Bangladesh, Afghanistan and Pakistan who entered the country without valid travel documents, citing religious persecution, to obtain visas to continue staying there.
The Indian Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) amended the Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) Order, 2025, through a notification issued on Wednesday, reports The Hindu.
The amendment requires Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians from the three countries who entered India on or before December 31, 2024, to obtain an appropriate visa for their continued stay.
The provision applies to those who entered India without valid travel documents or whose documents have since expired, after being compelled to seek shelter due to religious persecution or fear of persecution.
The amendment retains an exemption introduced through a September 2, 2025 notification, which allowed members of the six communities to enter and stay in India without valid passports or visas.
However, the latest notification states that they must obtain an appropriate category of visa after entering India to continue their stay.
The 2025 exemption was issued under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, consolidating earlier notifications that exempted members of the communities from prosecution under passport and foreigners laws.
The amendment also aligns the exempted categories with India's Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, which provides a pathway to citizenship for members of the six non-Muslim communities from the three neighbouring countries who entered India before December 31, 2014.
The amendment also revises provisions governing travel between India, Nepal and Bhutan, introduces a formal definition of the Visa Manual and reorganises several categories of exemptions for foreign nationals.
The Visa Manual is defined as a central government-issued document containing instructions on visas, immigration and related matters.
Indian citizens travelling to Nepal or Bhutan, as well as Nepali and Bhutanese citizens entering or leaving India, will now have to produce identity documents specified in the manual before immigration authorities.
The passport exemption will not apply to Indian citizens using the Indo-Nepal or Indo-Bhutan borders to travel to third countries. Such travellers must carry valid passports and use designated immigration checkpoints.
Similarly, Nepali and Bhutanese citizens travelling to destinations other than India, Nepal or Bhutan, or those who have embarked from or transited through China, Macau, Hong Kong or Pakistan, must possess valid passports and visas.

90 million displaced people at climate risk in Bangladesh, other countries: UNHCR
item.description:
REFUGEES-CLIMATE/UN

Nearly 90 million forcibly displaced people are living in countries increasingly exposed to climate-related droughts, floods and extreme heat, the UN refugee agency said on Friday, warning ahead of the COP31 climate summit that more funding is needed to help vulnerable communities adapt.

Nearly three-quarters of the world's forcibly displaced people are living in countries such as Afghanistan and Bangladesh that are exposed to severe climate-related risks, according to the report by the agency, known as UNHCR, published ahead of the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey. The findings show the overlap between conflict, displacement and climate change, the report said.

"Climate adaptation in fragile and displacement-affected areas is a matter of survival," said Anton Leis Garcia, UNHCR's assistant high commissioner for operations.

"We need climate financing to reach the communities where the needs are greatest," he said.

The report highlighted the experience of a Sudanese refugee who fled conflict in al-Fashir in June 2023 to the Farchana refugee settlement in eastern Chad. The refugee said she sometimes goes a week without finding safe water and must walk increasingly long distances for alternative sources as nearby seasonal riverbeds dry up amid intensifying heat.

Returns at risk

It also warned that climate change is making it harder for displaced people to return home sustainably.

In the first half of 2026, more than two-thirds of refugee returns were to countries highly exposed to climate hazards, placing them at risk of renewed displacement, the report said.

In Syria, where nearly 4 million displaced people have recently returned, people face worsening water scarcity and erratic rainfall, while flooding along the Euphrates River in May damaged homes and displaced thousands of people, the report said.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, one in three refugee settlements could experience at least 100 days of dangerous heat each year by 2050, threatening health and livelihoods, the report said. In some settlements in Ethiopia, including Helaweyn, dangerous heat could persist for more than 200 days a year, increasing the risks of heatstroke and premature death.

"Refugees often have limited access to cooling, water and reliable energy, making it harder to escape dangerous temperatures," the report said.

UNHCR also warned that a forecast supersized El Niño could worsen climate-related risks in many refugee-hosting countries and trigger further displacement.

In East Africa, severe flooding could displace up to 3 million people in Somalia, Kenya, South Sudan and Uganda by the end of this year, UNHCR said. In the Sahel, drought, flooding and conflict could intensify competition over scarce resources, while parts of Asia face heightened risks of droughts, floods and cyclones.

UNHCR called on governments and climate-finance institutions meeting at COP31 to increase funding for climate adaptation, highlighting that only about 10 per cent of climate finance reaches fragile or conflict-affected countries.

On Wednesday, a separate UN report found rich ​countries were falling well short of the $305 billion needed each year ‌to help developing nations adapt to climate change, even as extreme weather events become more frequent and severe.

item.title: Dengue: 3 more die, 1,535 hospitalized in 24hrs
item.description:
Three dengue patients died in the last 24 hours till 8:00 am on Friday while 1,535 were hospitalized after being infected with the mosquito-borne disease during the same period.
The latest fatalities have raised the country's dengue death toll to 455 this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of the newly-hospitalized dengue patients, 721 were in Dhaka Division, 88 in Mymensingh Division, 275 in Chittagong Division, 161 in Khulna Division, 104 in Rajshahi Division, 43 in Rangpur Division and 143 in Barisal Division.
According to the report, a total of 145,906 dengue patients have, so far, been hospitalized across the country this year.
So far, 139,678 dengue patients have recovered and returned home after receiving treatment in the hospitals.
A total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and 413 people died from the mosquito-borne disease last year.
